claims.text: The starting nanoparticles are solid, equiatomic Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy alloys with an initially homogeneous elemental distribution.
Local atomic segregation into compositionally distinct regions governs the onset and progression of premelting and melting.
Compositionally segregated regions melt at lower temperatures than more homogeneous regions.
Heating produces emergent nanoscale compositional heterogeneities.
The compositional heterogeneities modify the local bonding environment.
The compositional heterogeneities locally reduce cohesive energy.
During heating, minor thermodynamic fluctuations drive separation of the constituent metal species.
Localized deviations from equiatomic composition lower the local melting point.
Locally depressed melting points generate early liquid-like behavior that spreads as temperature increases.
Regions with measurable compositional segregation will show softening or surface atomic mobility at lower temperatures than uniformly composed control nanoparticles.
Segregated nanoparticles will have a broader melting-temperature distribution than particles lacking segregation.
Ag, Au, Al, and Pd monometallic nanoparticles have relatively uniform and well-characterized melting behavior.
Segregation-mediated behavior requires atomic diffusion to be sufficiently active during heating.
The proposed mechanism may not apply to substantially different elemental combinations, particle sizes, or synthesis conditions that suppress segregation.
Direct evidence connecting nanoscale segregation to melting onset in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles is sparse.
The hypothesis is extrapolated from analogous observations in simpler material systems.
